summary:
Vasant Kearney argues that AI in healthcare claims should be grounded in X12, treated as a harness rather than a file format. He sketches a brief AI history from CNNs through transformers to modern agentic tools, and warns against flattening multimodal records, fully hardcoding long workflows, and relying on local-disk memory the way coding agents do. Instead, enterprise memory must live in a database for logical separation, and a stronger model cannot simply be swapped in because benchmark gains do not transfer automatically to a system built around the prior model.

He defines a harness broadly as everything surrounding agentic reasoning: memory, tools, checks, permissions, handoffs, evals, and, in healthcare claims, X12. X12 functions like a strict language such as COBOL or TypeScript, giving LLMs the confinement they need so outputs can be validated and rejected when wrong. He walks through the claim lifecycle, from scheduling and treatment through documents, submission, acknowledgement (the 999), and payment (the 835), noting that every stage, including phone calls and portal sessions, corresponds to a public X12 transaction such as the 270 eligibility request, which agents can look up rather than invent.

Crucially, he emphasizes that no payer surface is ground truth: the phone system, web portal, and X12 layer are often built by different teams or contractors and can disagree or agree on the wrong answer, so X12 information can be wrong or updated later. He therefore normalizes all inputs into an internal, semi-correct X12 representation that holds only until downstream evidence disproves it, using subsequent treatments and imaging, such as CBCT slices, as evidentiary anchors. He closes by advocating a posture that is AI-pilled and AI-skeptical at once, deploying small, cost-effective models conservatively, because we can set models up to fail and routine, high-volume tasks must remain affordable.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: X12 should be treated as a harness, not a file format, because strict, public schemas give LLMs the confinement they need to be validated and rejected when wrong.
Phone calls, web portals, and X12 feeds are built by different teams or contractors, so they can disagree or jointly assert the wrong answer; no payer surface is ground truth.
Normalize all payer inputs into an internal, semi-correct X12 representation that holds only until downstream evidence (e.g., treatments, imaging such as CBCT slices) proves it otherwise.
The full claim lifecycle has public X12 correspondences: scheduling, treatment, the 275 attachment, submission, the 999 acknowledgement, the 835 payment, and 270 eligibility checks.
Enterprise healthcare memory must live in a database, not local disk, for logical separation from the user.
A stronger model on benchmarks is not automatically better inside an existing system; evals and validation must be rebuilt before any swap.
Long, multimodal agentic chains (e.g., 50 steps) are expensive and error-prone, so the right balance lies between pure reasoning and hardcoded logic.
Persistent per-user memory helps with routine workflows but must allow users to break out to avoid steering bias.
Be simultaneously AI-pilled and AI-skeptical: deploy small, cost-effective models conservatively, because we can set models up to fail and routine tasks run at high volume.
Explain why X12 functions as a harness for AI agents in healthcare claims rather than just a file format, and why it is a system of rules rather than ground truth.

sections.title: Reading the room and setting goals
sections.summary: Kearney polls the audience on healthcare, agentic workflows, and production models, then frames the talk around lowering insurance-interaction cost and improving patient experience.

sections.title: From CNNs to the agentic execution layer
sections.summary: He traces AI from CNNs and unsupervised learning through transformers and chat LLMs to modern agentic systems, and introduces the handwritten-digit-to-check analogy to show a solved subproblem is not a working harness.

sections.title: Multimodal context and desktop use
sections.summary: He warns that flattening a multimodal record into findings or geometries can lose context needed by downstream procedures, and notes that multimodal processing is still required for healthcare desktop use.

sections.title: What the agentic execution layer touches
sections.summary: He defines the layer as a model's ability to take consequential actions (database and code queries, insurance transactions, phone calls, portals, EHRs) that produce user logs, and contrasts local memory with database memory for enterprise.

sections.title: Model swaps and the need for a harness
sections.summary: He argues a stronger benchmark model is not automatically better inside an existing system, requiring rebuilt evals and validation, and defines a harness broadly to include memory, tools, checks, permissions, handoffs, evals, and X12.

sections.title: X12 as guardrail over 50-step chains
sections.summary: He compares X12 to strict languages like COBOL and TypeScript that help LLMs thrive under confinement, and balances pure agentic reasoning against fully hardcoded workflows, while introducing partner-, organization-, and user-level memory and its bias risks.

sections.title: The claim lifecycle as X12 correspondence
sections.summary: He walks through scheduling, treatment, documents (including the 275 imaging attachment), submission, and payment, and stresses that phone calls and portal sessions all map to public X12 transactions like the 270 eligibility request.

sections.title: Public schema lets agents look it up
sections.summary: He closes the section by reiterating the transactions and noting that X12 schemas are public, so agents can look them up instead of inventing ad hoc schemas.

sections.title: X12 as rules, not ground truth
sections.summary: He emphasizes that payer phone systems, portals, and X12 layers are often built by separate teams or contractors and can disagree or jointly assert the wrong coverage, so any X12 from a payer can be wrong or updated later.

sections.title: Normalizing to an internal semi-correct X12
sections.summary: He shows that regardless of origin, payer inputs are normalized into an internal semi-correct X12 held only until downstream evidence (such as treatments or CBCT imaging slices) disproves it, and traces the claim progression through submission, the 999 acknowledgement, the 835 receipt of payment, and status verification.

sections.title: Be AI-pilled and AI-skeptical
sections.summary: He closes by urging a dual posture: enthusiastic about AI's potential but skeptical in deployment, using small, cost-effective models conservatively for high-volume routine healthcare tasks because we can set models up to fail.

limitations: Flattening multimodal records loses context relevant to downstream procedures.
Fully hardcoding 50-step agentic workflows produces bloated, unmaintainable code requiring large engineering teams.
Persistent memory across chats and days can steer users toward repeating yesterday's behavior.
Local-disk memory like Claude Code/Codex is unsuitable for enterprise healthcare workflows.
Payer phone, portal, and X12 surfaces are often built by different teams or contractors and can agree on the wrong answer.
X12 data from payers can be wrong at any time or updated later, so it is never ground truth.
Overpowered, expensive models are unsuitable for high-volume routine healthcare workflows.
We can inadvertently design and set up models to fail.
quantitativeClaims: 50 steps as an example length for a healthcare agentic workflow
Routine tasks that 'need to be done a thousand times a day' as a high-volume example

organization.name: Onlay
organization.summary: Onlay (Onlay AI) is a dental revenue-cycle company founded by Vasant Kearney. First-party pages describe one continuous system for eligibility, end-to-end billing, collections, and denial recovery, connected to the practice-management, clearinghouse, and payer workflows clinics already use. The legal footer identifies Curaclear Inc. DBA Onlay AI. The talk presents Onlay's X12-as-harness approach for healthcare claims agents, not the X12 standards body itself.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. onlay.ai homepage and demo page are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
